thesis: A rule-bound caseworker sent to judge a house of magical children discovers that a family is something you choose — and that he is allowed to choose it too.

nodes.title: Talia
nodes.remind: A fierce, bearded gnome who tends the island's garden and threatens to bury people in it.
nodes.deeper: Talia's prickliness is protection. Her garden is the first place Linus is truly welcomed, and tending things that grow becomes the book's picture of patient care.
nodes.q: What does Talia's garden say about how the children were treated before?

nodes.title: Theodore
nodes.remind: A small wyvern who hoards buttons as treasure and speaks in chirps.
nodes.deeper: Theodore's gift of a button to Linus is one of the book's quiet turning points: trust offered in the only currency he values.
nodes.q: Why does such a small gift mean so much to Linus?

nodes.title: Phee
nodes.remind: A forest sprite who grows trees and is learning the limits of her power.
nodes.deeper: Phee's lessons with Zoe show the orphanage as a place where magic is taught, not feared.
seen: Practising with Zoe in the woods
nodes.q: How does the island treat magic differently from the city?

nodes.title: Lucy
nodes.remind: Six years old, possibly the Antichrist, devoted to old records.
nodes.deeper: Lucy is the Department's greatest fear and the book's best joke: a terrifying label on a child who mostly wants music and to be loved. His bond with Linus grows over records.
nodes.q: Is Lucy defined by what he is or by how he's raised?

nodes.title: Chauncey
nodes.remind: A green, tentacled blob whose dearest dream is to be a hotel bellhop.
nodes.deeper: Chauncey's ordinary dream in an extraordinary body is the book's gentlest argument against prejudice: everyone wants to be useful and seen.
nodes.q: Why is Chauncey's dream so moving precisely because it's ordinary?

nodes.title: Sal
nodes.remind: A quiet boy who turns into a Pomeranian when frightened; he writes.
nodes.deeper: Sal has been moved between homes more than any of the children. His slow trust in Linus, and his writing, show what safety makes possible.
nodes.q: What finally lets Sal feel safe?

nodes.title: Linus Baker
nodes.remind: A lonely DICOMY caseworker who lives by the rulebook.
nodes.deeper: Linus begins as an observer whose job is to stay objective. His arc is the book's: from following rules that keep him safe and small, to choosing a life that is messy and his own.
nodes.q: When did you first sense Linus had stopped being an observer?

nodes.title: Rules & Regs
nodes.remind: The thick DICOMY handbook Linus quotes when anxious.
nodes.deeper: The handbook stands for a life lived by other people's permission. Linus doesn't throw it away so much as outgrow it.
nodes.q: Which rule did Linus most need to break?

nodes.title: The gray city
nodes.remind: Linus's rainy, colourless home and office.
nodes.deeper: Klune draws the city in gray and the island in colour; going back to the city after the island shows Linus what he can no longer accept.
nodes.q: What does the colour of each place tell you?

nodes.title: Arthur
nodes.remind: The calm, wry master of the Marsyas Island orphanage.
nodes.deeper: Arthur is a phoenix who hides his fire because the world fears what it can't control. Once an orphan kept out of sight, he runs the house as the home he never had.
nodes.q: When does hiding protect people, and when does it cost them?

nodes.title: Zoe
nodes.remind: The sprite whose magic protects the island, and Arthur's ally.
nodes.deeper: Zoe guards the island and teaches the children; her steadiness shows Arthur hasn't done this alone.
nodes.q: What role does Zoe play in making the house safe?

nodes.title: Found family
nodes.remind: Six unwanted children, a guardian and a caseworker choose each other.
nodes.deeper: Family is built from small rituals — dinners, music, a button, a picnic — and is something you keep choosing.
seen: Dinners where every child is heard
nodes.q: Which small moment made the household feel like a family to you?

nodes.title: Prejudice & fear
nodes.remind: The villagers and the Department fear the children for what they are.
nodes.deeper: The book shows prejudice as bureaucratic as much as personal, and answers it with ordinary kindness.
nodes.q: Where does the book locate the real danger?

nodes.title: Choosing kindness
nodes.remind: Kindness as a decision, made again and again.
nodes.deeper: Klune's gentlest claim: kindness is a form of resistance.
nodes.q: Is kindness in this book naive, or brave?

nodes.title: Rules vs. living
nodes.remind: A safe, rule-bound life against a full one.
nodes.deeper: Linus must decide whether the rules serve people or the other way round.
nodes.q: What would you have written in Linus's report?

nodes.title: Marsyas Island
nodes.remind: The island orphanage, bright with colour and the sea.
nodes.deeper: The island is the book's idea of home made physical.
nodes.q: What makes Marsyas feel like home?

nodes.title: The wary village
nodes.remind: The mainland town that fears the children.
nodes.deeper: The village shows prejudice up close — and who is willing to change.

nodes.title: DICOMY
nodes.remind: The Department in Charge of Magical Youth.
nodes.deeper: Extremely Upper Management embodies institutional fear dressed as care.
nodes.q: Who benefits from the Department's rules?

timeline.title: The assignment
timeline.summary: Linus is sent by Extremely Upper Management to inspect a classified orphanage for a month.

timeline.title: Arriving on the island
timeline.summary: He meets Arthur, Zoe and six magical children.

timeline.title: Getting to know them
timeline.summary: Records with Lucy, gardens with Talia, buttons with Theodore.

timeline.title: The village
timeline.summary: A trip to town shows the islanders' fear, and who is kind anyway.

timeline.title: Arthur's secret
timeline.summary: Linus learns what Arthur is and what was done to him.

timeline.title: The report
timeline.summary: The month ends; Linus writes what he saw and returns to the city.

timeline.title: Choosing
timeline.summary: Back home, Linus realizes where he belongs.
